scenario.name: Microsoft & CISA DFIR — SMB ADMIN$ Share, PSEXESVC Named Pipe & Service Install Forensics (EID 5145 / 7045)
scenario.overview: Picture a stately national art museum gallery with framed paintings on marble walls, velvet stanchion ropes, illuminated glass display pedestals, and thin security laser beams. Inside the hushed art museum hall, a thief studies how the velvet stanchions and glass pedestal sensors respond to routine curator maintenance checks. In this real-world scenario, the intruder bypasses the normal inspection rule to reach the laser-guarded glass display case, then smuggles copied records out past the velvet rope gallery entrance in tiny disguised batches. During closing inspection, the museum curator checks the gallery motion-sensor log and spots a brief laser shadow that never matched any scheduled restoration. In this scenario (T1021.002, Microsoft & CISA DFIR, SMB ADMIN$ Share, PSEXESVC Named Pipe & Service Install Forensics , EID 5145 / 7045), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: sMB ADMIN$ Share Write, then remote Service Installation via SCM, then named Pipe Stdin/Stdout/Stderr Redirection. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering SMB ADMIN$ Share Write, then Remote Service Installation via SCM, then Named Pipe Stdin/Stdout/Stderr Redirection, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 17 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: Stage 1: SMB ADMIN$ Share Write & IPC$ svcctl RPC Bind (Security EventID 5140 & 5145)
stages.subtitle: Lateral Movement (T1021.002 - Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares)
stages.description: Inside the hushed art museum hall, a thief studies how the velvet stanchions and glass pedestal sensors respond to routine curator maintenance checks. Specifically in Step 1, the intruder bypasses the normal inspection rule to reach the laser-guarded glass display case while everyday visitors and the museum curator go about their routine. The attacker executes PsExec.exe \\10.10.20.15 -s cmd.exe. The target host logs Security EventID 5140 (Network share object accessed) and EventID 5145 (Detailed File Share Access) showing WriteData (AccessMask 0x2) of PSEXESVC.exe into the \\*\ADMIN$ share (C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe), followed by an IPC$ access to the svcctl named pipe (logged in WinEvent Event 5145 with EventID=5145 , Detailed File Share Audit, ShareName=\\*\ADMIN$ , C:\Windows, RelativeTargetName=PSEXESVC.exe, AccessMask=0x2 , WriteData so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). Under the hood, the observed step executes PsExec.exe -accepteula \\10.10.20.15 -s cmd.exe (which Uploads a service binary , such as PSEXESVC.exe over SMB2/3 to the target's administrative \\<target>\ADMIN$ share , C:\Windows\, opens the \\<targ so that executes lateral movement with immediate NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges on the remote host , T1021.002 during "SMB ADMIN$ Share Write & IPC$ svcctl RPC Bind , Security EventID 5140 & 5145", leaving correlated forensic traces in Security EventID 5145, System EventID 7045, and Sysmon EventID 17/18). Next, the follow-up artifact Security EventID 5145: ShareName=\\*\ADMIN$ RelativeTargetName=PSEXESVC.exe AccessMask=0x2 (WriteData) runs (which Uploads a service binary , such as PSEXESVC.exe over SMB2/3 to the target's administrative \\<target>\ADMIN$ share , C:\Windows\, opens the \\<targ so that executes lateral movement with immediate NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges on the remote host , T1021.002 during "SMB ADMIN$ Share Write & IPC$ svcctl RPC Bind , Security EventID 5140 & 5145", leaving correlated forensic traces in Security EventID 5145, System EventID 7045, and Sysmon EventID 17/18). stages.title: Stage 2: Remote Service Installation via SCM CreateServiceW (System EventID 7045 & Security EventID 4697)
stages.subtitle: Execution (T1569.002 - System Services: Service Execution)
stages.description: Using a mirror-angle trick that satisfies the glass case laser beam, the thief lifts the cover and swaps a priceless artifact for a weight-matched replica. Here in Step 2 inside the art museum, the intruder bypasses the normal inspection rule to reach the laser-guarded glass display case without disturbing the permanent restoration wing. Over the \pipe\svcctl RPC interface, the Service Control Manager (services.exe) invokes CreateServiceW and logs System EventID 7045 (A service was installed in the system) and Security EventID 4697 with ServiceName="PSEXESVC", ImagePath="%SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe", ServiceType="user mode service" (0x10), and StartType="demand start" (0x3) (logged in WinEvent Event 7045 with EventID=7045 , System SCM / 4697 , Security, ServiceName=PSEXESVC, ServiceFileName=%SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe, ServiceAccount=LocalSystem so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). Under the hood, the observed step executes RPC svcctl: RCreateServiceW(lpServiceName="PSEXESVC", lpBinaryPathName="%SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe") (which Uploads a service binary , such as PSEXESVC.exe over SMB2/3 to the target's administrative \\<target>\ADMIN$ share , C:\Windows\, opens the \\<targ so that executes lateral movement with immediate NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges on the remote host , T1569.002 during "Remote Service Installation via SCM CreateServiceW , System EventID 7045 & Security EventID 4697", leaving correlated forensic traces in Security EventID 5145, System EventID 7045, and Sysmon EventID 17/18). Next, the follow-up artifact System EventID 7045: Service Name=PSEXESVC, Service File Name=%SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe, Account Name=LocalSystem runs (which Uploads a service binary , such as PSEXESVC.exe over SMB2/3 to the target's administrative \\<target>\ADMIN$ share , C:\Windows\, opens the \\<targ so that executes lateral movement with immediate NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM privileges on the remote host , T1569.002 during "Remote Service Installation via SCM CreateServiceW , System EventID 7045 & Security EventID 4697", leaving correlated forensic traces in Security EventID 5145, System EventID 7045, and Sysmon EventID 17/18). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ %SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe / ⇠#2 ACK 7045) from Node ② (#2 Core Identity & VLAN Switch) to Node ③ (#3 SMB :445 ADMIN$ & IPC$ Share), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 PSEXESVC.exe & Named Pipes).

stages.title: Stage 3: Named Pipe Stdin/Stdout/Stderr Redirection (Sysmon EventID 17 & 18)
stages.subtitle: Execution (T1569.002 - Sysmon EventID 17/18 Named Pipe Forensics)
stages.description: The glass pedestal seals back down without tripping the lobby bell, leaving visitors admiring a convincing decoy behind the velvet ropes. In this final step inside the art museum, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the velvet rope gallery entrance in tiny disguised batches until the gallery motion-sensor console catches the mismatch. Even if the attacker renames the binary using PsExec -r, PSEXESVC.exe creates a control pipe and three I/O redirection named pipes matching \PSEXESVC-<Host>-<PID>-stdin, -stdout, and -stderr. Sysmon EventID 17 (PipeCreated) and EventID 18 (PipeConnected) capture the exact PipeName and Image regardless of service renaming (logged in Sysmon Event 17 with EventID=17 , PipeCreated / 18 , PipeConnected, Image=C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe, PipeNamePattern=\PSEXESVC-<HOST>-<PID>-{stdin,stdout,stderr}, SpawnedChildProcess=C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe , NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). Under the hood, the observed step executes Sysmon EventID 17 (PipeCreated): PipeName=\PSEXESVC-WKS04-3104-stdin (which executes the technical command / telemetry directive , Sysmon EventID 17 , PipeCreated: PipeName=\PSEXESVC-WKS04-3104-stdin via System / Runtime Ex so that advances the scenario kill-chain under MITRE T1569.002 during "Named Pipe Stdin/Stdout/Stderr Redirection , Sysmon EventID 17 & 18" , Even if the attacker renames the binary using PsExec -r, PSEXESVC while generating verifiable host or network telemetry for DFIR attribution). Next, the follow-up artifact Sysmon EventID 17 (PipeCreated): PipeName=\PSEXESVC-WKS04-3104-stdout runs (which executes the technical command / telemetry directive , Sysmon EventID 17 , PipeCreated: PipeName=\PSEXESVC-WKS04-3104-stdout via System / Runtime E so that advances the scenario kill-chain under MITRE T1569.002 during "Named Pipe Stdin/Stdout/Stderr Redirection , Sysmon EventID 17 & 18" , Even if the attacker renames the binary using PsExec -r, PSEXESVC while generating verifiable host or network telemetry for DFIR attribution). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe creating \PSEXESVC-WKS04-3104-stdin / ⇠#3 ACK 17) from Node ③ (#3 SMB :445 ADMIN$ & IPC$ Share) to Node ④ (#4 services.exe (SCM PID 612)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 PSEXESVC.exe & Named Pipes).
